scenes.title: HAVING
scenes.narration: HAVING filters groups after aggregation, doing for GROUP BY what WHERE does for rows.

scenes.title: Filtering groups
scenes.narration: HAVING filters the groups produced by GROUP BY based on their aggregate values. It runs after the grouping and aggregation have completed. This lets it reference functions like COUNT and SUM, which WHERE cannot do.

scenes.title: Departments over ten people
scenes.code:
SELECT department, COUNT(*) AS headcount
FROM employees
GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 10;
scenes.narration: GROUP BY forms one group per department and COUNT tallies each. HAVING then keeps only the groups whose count exceeds ten. The result lists just the departments with more than ten employees.

scenes.heading: WHERE vs HAVING
scenes.narration: WHERE filters raw rows before any grouping takes place and cannot reference aggregates. HAVING filters the groups afterward and is built to test aggregate values. Using them together lets you filter both the input rows and the resulting groups.

scenes.text: Use WHERE to filter rows and HAVING to filter groups, often in the same query.
scenes.narration: Filter rows with WHERE and filter aggregated groups with HAVING, combining both when you need to narrow the input and the summary.
